video_metadata.working_title: Medgar Evers: How a Widow and Secret Files Solved a 31-Year Cold Case | Mississippi 1963
video_metadata.topic_one_sentence: Civil rights leader Medgar Evers, 37, was shot in the back in his Jackson, Mississippi driveway on June 12, 1963; the man whose fingerprint was on the rifle scope walked free after two hung juries in 1964, and only the persistence of his widow Myrlie, a reporter's discovery in secret state files and a prosecutor who rebuilt a lost case brought a conviction on February 5, 1994.
video_metadata.primary_emotion_to_evoke: Dignified grief turning into quiet outrage at a system that protected a killer, then hard-won justice.

protagonist._instructions: Narrative protagonist is the victim and his widow; the convicted killer is described in the suspect fields below.
protagonist.occupation_or_status: First NAACP field secretary for Mississippi (from 1954); World War II Army veteran
protagonist.location: Family home on Guynes Street (today Margaret Walker Alexander Drive), Jackson, Mississippi
protagonist.physical_description: Not used in script beyond archival photos.
protagonist.background_brief: Born in Decatur, Mississippi, the son of farmer and sawmill worker James Evers and his wife Jesse. Left high school at 17 to enlist in the segregated U.S. Army; served in France and Germany after D-Day; honorably discharged 1946. Attended Alcorn A&M College, married classmate Myrlie Beasley on December 24, 1951, graduated 1952. Applied to the University of Mississippi law school in 1954 after Brown v. Board and was denied; the NAACP then made him its first Mississippi field secretary. Investigated racial violence (including the 1955 Emmett Till case), organized voter registration and boycotts, supported James Meredith's 1962 admission to Ole Miss, and led the 1963 Jackson Movement.
protagonist.psychological_profile: Described by contemporaries and the National Park Service as disciplined, determined and aware of the danger; the family practiced what to do if the house was attacked.
protagonist.mundane_humanizing_detail: He called Myrlie on June 11, 1963 and urged her to watch President Kennedy's civil rights speech on television; she and the children waited up for him that night.

convicted_person.born: November 9, 1920, Sacramento, California; raised in Greenwood, Mississippi
convicted_person.background: U.S. Marine in World War II; fertilizer salesman in Greenwood; white segregationist and member of the White Citizens' Council (background knowledge, widely documented).
convicted_person.legal_status: Convicted of murder by a Hinds County jury February 5, 1994; sentenced to life by Judge L. Breland Hilburn; conviction affirmed by the Mississippi Supreme Court on December 22, 1997; died in custody January 21, 2001, age 80, at the University Medical Center in Jackson.
convicted_person.position_on_guilt: Denied the killing; in 1964 he testified the rifle could have been his but he was not sure [38].

individuals.name: Medgar Evers
individuals.specific_impact_suffered: Shot in the back in his driveway just after midnight on June 12, 1963; died at University Hospital in Jackson less than an hour later from trauma and blood loss [1][6].
individuals.humanizing_detail: Arrived home carrying T-shirts reading 'Jim Crow Must Go' [29][43].
individuals.any_quotes_from_them: 'You can kill a man, but you can't kill an idea.' (widely attributed; see notes)

individuals.name: Myrlie Evers (later Myrlie Evers-Williams)
individuals.specific_impact_suffered: Found her husband collapsed in the carport; testified in both 1964 trials; spent three decades pressing for the case to be reopened [1][12][27].
individuals.any_quotes_from_them: 'Yes, Medgar!' on hearing the verdict, February 5, 1994 [26][27].

individuals.name: Darrell Kenyatta Evers
individuals.specific_impact_suffered: Was in the house during the shooting; died in 2001 [36].
individuals.humanizing_detail: Spelled Darrell or Darryl in different sources.

individuals.name: Reena Denise Evers
individuals.specific_impact_suffered: In the house during the shooting; in court with her mother for the 1994 verdict (AP photo caption) [27].

individuals.name: James Van Dyke Evers
individuals.specific_impact_suffered: The older children helped the 3-year-old into the bathtub during the attack [1]; reported to have seen his father's body at the 1991 exhumation [24].

collective_victims_if_applicable.group_description: Black Mississippians denied the vote and equal justice under Jim Crow
collective_victims_if_applicable.total_number_affected: Not quantified in script beyond the voter-registration figure

characters.name: Jerry Mitchell
characters.key_actions_they_took: Obtained leaked Mississippi State Sovereignty Commission records and reported on October 1, 1989 that the state agency had screened prospective jurors for Beckwith's defense during the 1964 retrial [19][20][21].
characters.notable_quotes: Said that when his story ran, 'the odds were literally more than a million to one' against the case being reopened [19].

characters.name: Bobby DeLaughter
characters.role_in_story: Hinds County assistant district attorney who prosecuted the 1994 trial
characters.key_actions_they_took: Agreed to reexamine the case at Myrlie Evers's request; recovered the 1964 transcripts, crime-scene photos and the missing murder weapon [12][17].

characters.name: Michael Baden
characters.key_actions_they_took: Performed the autopsy on Medgar Evers's exhumed body in 1991; said the body was still intact [24][25].

characters.name: L. Breland Hilburn
characters.key_actions_they_took: Presided over the 1994 trial and imposed the life sentence [13][42].

characters.name: Ross Barnett
characters.key_actions_they_took: Came into the courtroom during a 1964 trial and greeted Beckwith while Myrlie Evers was testifying, according to accounts; sources differ on handshake versus embrace [33][7].

characters.name: Mary Ann Adams, Peggy Morgan, Dan Prince, Elluard 'Dick' Davis (and others)
characters.key_actions_they_took: Testified that Beckwith had spoken of the killing over the years; the defense attacked Prince as a drunk with a grudge over an eviction [10].

characters.name: John F. Kennedy
characters.key_actions_they_took: Delivered a televised civil rights address on the evening of June 11, 1963, hours before the shooting [28].
characters.notable_quotes: 'We are confronted primarily with a moral issue. It is as old as the scriptures and is as clear as the American Constitution.' [28]

events.what_happened: Medgar Wiley Evers is born.
events.significance: Victim's origin; the Civil Rights Act would be signed on his birthday in 1964.

events.what_happened: Evers serves in the segregated U.S. Army after leaving high school at 17; honorable discharge 1946.
events.significance: Veteran denied rights at home; later buried at Arlington.

events.what_happened: Evers marries Alcorn classmate Myrlie Beasley; he graduates in 1952.
After Brown v. Board of Education, Evers applies to the University of Mississippi law school and is denied; the NAACP hires him as its first Mississippi field secretary.
Legislature creates the Mississippi State Sovereignty Commission to defend segregation (background, widely documented).
events.significance: The agency whose files would later reopen the case.

events.what_happened: Evers delivers a televised address on segregation in Jackson (background; date per standard histories).
events.significance: Raised his profile and his danger.

events.what_happened: A firebomb is thrown at the Evers carport (background; standard histories).
events.significance: Prior attack; family had rehearsed safety drills.

events.what_happened: President Kennedy's televised address on civil rights; Evers had urged Myrlie to watch it while he attended meetings.

events.date: June 12, 1963, just after midnight (about 12:40 a.m. per History.com)
events.what_happened: Evers pulls into his driveway carrying 'Jim Crow Must Go' T-shirts and is shot in the back with a rifle fired from a thicket across the street. Myrlie and the children, waiting up watching TV, hear the shot; the children drop to the floor as practiced.
Evers dies less than an hour after the shooting from trauma and blood loss.
Police recover a rifle (a 1917 Enfield .30-06 with a telescopic sight) in nearby brush, about 150 feet from the scene per one account; a fingerprint is on the scope.
events.significance: The evidence that named the suspect.

events.what_happened: The fingerprint on the scope is traced to Byron De La Beckwith of Greenwood; the rifle had been obtained in a 1960 trade with a friend; Beckwith is arrested and charged.
Funeral in Jackson; burial with full military honors at Arlington (June 19 date pending verification).
First trial; all-white, all-male jury deadlocks after deliberations reported at more than 30 hours; mistrial.

Second trial; again a hung jury. Two Greenwood police officers testify they saw Beckwith in Greenwood, more than 90 miles away. The Sovereignty Commission secretly screened prospective jurors for the defense.
Civil Rights Act signed, on what would have been Evers's 39th birthday (background).
Prosecution of the 1963 charge is dropped (background; widely reported).
Beckwith arrested in New Orleans with a bomb in his car in 1973; later convicted in Louisiana and imprisoned (background).
events.significance: Pattern; a prison guard from this period later testified (pending).

events.what_happened: Some Sovereignty Commission records become public after the ACLU lawsuit; Jerry Mitchell obtains about 2,400 pages.
Mitchell reports that the Sovereignty Commission helped Beckwith's defense by investigating potential jurors in the second trial.
At Myrlie Evers's request, DeLaughter reexamines the case; the 1964 transcripts, crime-scene photos and the rifle, missing from the evidence room, are recovered.
A grand jury indicts Beckwith again for the murder of Medgar Evers.
Beckwith, about 70 and living in Tennessee, fights extradition for about ten months before being returned to Mississippi.
Medgar Evers's body is exhumed and autopsied by Dr. Michael Baden, nearly 30 years after his death; Baden said the body was still intact.
events.significance: Modern forensic record for the new trial.

events.what_happened: Third trial before Judge L. Breland Hilburn; jury of eight Black and four white jurors (seven women, five men); prosecution relies on the rifle, the fingerprint on the scope, the 1964 transcripts and new witnesses.
Beckwith, 73, convicted of murder and sentenced to life in prison. Myrlie Evers-Williams: 'Yes, Medgar!'
Conviction affirmed 4-2; the court rejects the speedy-trial claim. Opinion by Justice Mike Mills.
Beckwith dies in custody at 80.
Evers family gives the home to Tougaloo College (1993); law creating the Medgar and Myrlie Evers Home National Monument signed (2019); NPS takes ownership in 2020 and the monument is established.
Medgar Evers posthumously awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom by President Biden.

the_moment.exact_location: Driveway and carport of the Evers home, Jackson, Mississippi
the_moment.what_is_happening: Medgar Evers, 37, steps out of his car carrying T-shirts that read 'Jim Crow Must Go'; inside, Myrlie and three children have waited up.
the_moment.what_makes_it_shocking: Hours earlier the President had called civil rights a moral issue on national television; the rifle was found almost immediately with a fingerprint on the scope, and still Mississippi did not convict for 31 years.
the_moment.ironic_twist: The mystery was never really who; it was whether a Mississippi jury would ever say it.

cold_open_material.central_mystery_question: How does a killer whose fingerprint is on the murder weapon stay free for thirty-one years, and what finally changed.

the_method._instructions: Adapted: legal and historical investigative methods rather than DNA.
the_method.technique_name: Reopening a civil-rights-era case: archival investigation, evidence recovery, exhumation and new witnesses
step_by_step_explanation: Fingerprint identification in 1963: the FBI compared the print on the telescopic sight with prints on file and traced it to Beckwith [8].
Tracing the weapon: the 1917 Enfield had come to Beckwith through a 1960 trade with a friend [38].
Secret state files: leaked Sovereignty Commission records showed the agency screened prospective jurors for the defense in 1964, giving a legal and moral reason to revisit the case [19][21].
Recovering lost evidence: transcripts of the 1964 trials, crime-scene photographs and the rifle itself, missing from the evidence room, were located [17].
Exhumation and autopsy: the body was exhumed and examined by Dr. Michael Baden in 1991 to create a modern medical record [24][25].
New witnesses: people who said Beckwith had talked about the killing in the years after 1964 testified in 1994 [10].
A representative jury: eight Black and four white jurors in 1994, unlike the all-white juries of 1964 [12][27].
the_method.why_it_worked: The physical evidence had always pointed one way; what changed was access to the evidence, proof of how the earlier juries had been manipulated, new testimony, and a jury drawn from the whole community.

technical_terms_to_explain.simple_explanation: Jurors cannot agree unanimously, so the trial ends with no verdict and the state may try again.
The prosecutor formally stops pursuing the case, without an acquittal.
Lifting a buried body under court authority so it can be examined again.
A defendant's argument that delay itself made a fair trial impossible; rejected here in 1997.
No one can be tried twice after a verdict; hung juries produce no verdict, so a new trial remained possible (background legal principle).

the_method.scale_of_operation: About 2,400 pages of Sovereignty Commission records obtained by Mitchell; three trials over 30 years.

systemic_failure.institution_that_failed: Mississippi's Jim Crow justice system and the Mississippi State Sovereignty Commission
systemic_failure.how_they_were_supposed_to_protect: Investigate and prosecute murder fairly with impartial juries.
systemic_failure.why_they_failed: All-white juries in a state where few Black citizens could register to vote and serve; a state-funded agency secretly helped the defense; political leaders openly sided with the accused.
specific_incompetence_examples: Two all-white juries deadlocked in 1964 despite the fingerprint on the scope [9][12].
The Sovereignty Commission screened prospective jurors for the defense [19][21].
Former governor Ross Barnett greeted the defendant in court during Myrlie Evers's testimony [33].
The murder weapon and records went missing from official custody for decades [17].
systemic_failure.ironic_details_about_the_failure: The physical evidence was found within hours and the suspect arrested within about ten days; the delay was entirely institutional.

the_investigation.investigating_agency: Jackson Police Department and FBI (1963); Hinds County District Attorney's Office (1989-1994)
the_investigation.initial_wrong_assumptions: Not a case of wrong suspects; the obstacle was the defense alibi from two Greenwood police officers and all-white juries.
the_investigation.key_breakthrough: Mitchell's October 1, 1989 story on the Sovereignty Commission's jury screening, followed by DeLaughter's recovery of the rifle and transcripts and the emergence of new witnesses.
the_investigation.the_fatal_mistake: The fingerprint left on the telescopic sight, and Beckwith's later talk about the killing to others.
the_investigation.how_long_until_caught: Arrested within about ten days in 1963; convicted 30 years and almost 8 months later.

the_confrontation.scene_description: The jury returns a guilty verdict; Myrlie Evers-Williams and her daughter Reena are photographed cheering.
the_confrontation.ironic_or_absurd_details: Same courthouse city, same charge, same rifle as 1964; the difference was the jury.

charges_filed: Murder of Medgar Evers (indicted 1963; reindicted December 1990)
legal_resolution.notable_court_testimony: New witnesses testified Beckwith had spoken of the killing; the prosecution read testimony from the 1964 transcripts and presented the rifle and fingerprint [9][10].
legal_resolution.sentence_received: Life in prison (some sources add without parole)
legal_resolution.current_status: Closed. Beckwith died in custody January 21, 2001; the conviction was affirmed in 1997. No pending proceedings as of October 2026.

details: The President called civil rights a moral issue on television hours before the shot.
The weapon with the suspect's fingerprint was found almost immediately, yet two juries could not agree.
A state agency funded by taxpayers, including Black taxpayers, quietly helped vet jurors for the accused.
The Civil Rights Act was signed on July 2, 1964, Evers's birthday, less than three months after the second mistrial.
Beckwith died at the University Medical Center in Jackson, the medical center whose University Hospital is where Evers died in 1963 (pending verification of the explicit link).

key_locations.atmosphere: Family home under threat; drills rehearsed.
key_locations.relevant_details: Address Guynes Street, renamed Margaret Walker Alexander Drive.

key_locations.physical_description: Brush and vines where the rifle was found.
key_locations.relevant_details: Rifle about 150 feet away per one account.
Burial with full military honors; site of the 1991 exhumation.

universal_stakes.why_this_matters_to_viewer: Justice delayed by institutions, not by lack of evidence; shows that records, reporters and families can reopen what power closed.
universal_stakes.how_this_could_happen_to_them: Any case can be buried when the system protecting it is compromised.
universal_stakes.lesson_or_warning: Evidence keeps; memory keeps; the question is whether people keep asking.
universal_stakes.current_relevance: The case helped spark the reopening of other civil-rights-era killings; the Evers home is a national monument; Medal of Freedom 2024.

Jackson Movement; mass arrests, detainees held at the state fairgrounds; May 28 Woolworth sit-in attacked by white crowd
